title: The Frog-Prince
paragraphs: One fine evening a young princess put on her bonnet and clogs and went out for a walk alone in a wood. When she came to a cool spring of water that bubbled up in the middle of it, she sat down to rest for a while. In her hand she held a golden ball, her favorite plaything, and she kept tossing it up in the air and catching it again as it came down. After a while she threw it so high that she missed it. The ball bounced away and rolled along the ground until at last it dropped into the spring. The princess peered into the water after her ball, but the spring was so deep that she could not see the bottom. Then she began to lament her loss, saying, “Oh, if only I could have my ball back! I would give all my fine clothes and jewels and everything I own in the world.”

While she was speaking, a frog stuck his head out of the water and said, “Princess, why are you crying so bitterly?” “Oh,” she said, “what could you do for me, you nasty frog? My golden ball has fallen into the spring.” The frog said, “I don’t want your pearls or jewels or fine clothes. But if you will love me, and let me live with you, and eat from your golden plate, and sleep in your bed, then I will bring you your ball.” “What nonsense this silly frog is talking,” thought the princess. “He can never even get out of the spring to visit me, though he may be able to fetch my ball. So I’ll tell him he can have what he asks.” And she said to the frog, “All right. If you bring me my ball, I’ll do everything you ask.” The frog ducked his head and dived deep under the water. After a little while he came up again with the ball in his mouth and tossed it onto the edge of the spring. The moment the young princess saw her ball, she ran to pick it up, and she was so delighted to hold it again that she never thought of the frog and ran home with it as fast as she could. The frog called after her, “Wait, princess, and take me with you as you promised!” But she did not stop to hear a word.

The next day, just as the princess sat down to dinner, she heard a strange sound—tap, tap, plash, plash—as if something were climbing the marble staircase. Soon there was a soft knock at the door, and a little voice called out:

“Open the door, my princess dear,
Open the door, your true love’s here!
Remember the words that you and I said
By the cool spring in the greenwood shade.”

The princess ran to the door and opened it, and there was the frog, whom she had completely forgotten. She was badly frightened. She slammed the door shut as fast as she could and went back to her seat. The king, her father, saw that something had scared her and asked what was the matter. “There’s a nasty frog at the door,” she said. “He fetched my ball out of the spring for me this morning. I told him he could live with me here, because I thought he could never get out of the spring. But now he’s at the door, and he wants to come in.”
While she was speaking, the frog knocked at the door again and called:

“Open the door, my princess dear,
Open the door, your true love’s here!
Remember the words that you and I said
By the cool spring in the greenwood shade.”

Then the king said to the young princess, “You gave your word, so you must keep it. Go and let him in.” She did, and the frog hopped into the room and then straight across it—tap, tap, plash, plash—from one end to the other, until he reached the table where the princess sat. “Please lift me onto a chair,” he said to the princess, “and let me sit next to you.” As soon as she had done so, the frog said, “Push your plate closer so I can eat from it.” She did that too, and when he had eaten all he could, he said, “Now I’m tired. Carry me upstairs and put me in your bed.” The princess, though very unwilling, picked him up in her hand and set him on the pillow of her own bed, where he slept all night. As soon as it was light, he jumped up, hopped downstairs and left the house. “Well,” thought the princess, “at last he’s gone, and he won’t trouble me any more.”
But she was wrong. When night came again, she heard the same tapping at the door, and the frog was back, calling:

“Open the door, my princess dear,
Open the door, your true love’s here!
Remember the words that you and I said
By the cool spring in the greenwood shade.”

When the princess opened the door, the frog came in and slept on her pillow as before, until morning. On the third night he did the same. But when the princess woke the next morning, she was astonished to find, in place of the frog, a handsome prince standing at the head of her bed and gazing at her with the most beautiful eyes she had ever seen.

He told her that a spiteful fairy had enchanted him and turned him into a frog, and that he was doomed to stay that way until some princess lifted him out of the spring, let him eat from her plate and let him sleep on her bed for three nights. “You,” said the prince, “have broken the fairy’s cruel spell, and now I wish for nothing more than that you come with me to my father’s kingdom, where I will marry you and love you as long as you live.”

The young princess, as you can imagine, was quick to say “Yes” to all this. As they were speaking, a splendid coach drove up, drawn by eight beautiful horses with plumes of feathers on their heads and golden harness. Behind the coach rode the prince’s servant, faithful Heinrich, who had grieved so long and so bitterly over his dear master’s misfortune during the enchantment that his heart had nearly burst.

They said goodbye to the king and climbed into the coach with the eight horses, and all set off, full of joy and merriment, for the prince’s kingdom. They arrived safely, and there they lived happily for many years.
